knowledge_points.label: Benchmarking: warm up, synchronize, CUDA events, several trials
knowledge_points.statement: Benchmarking measures end-to-end wall-clock time and nothing finer; to make it mean something you warm up first (compilation, caches), call torch.cuda.synchronize() because kernel launches return before the GPU finishes, time with CUDA events, and average several trials.

anchors.quote: Benchmarking measures the wall-clock time of performing some operation. It only gives you end-to-end time, not where time is spent (profiling).
Warmup: first times might be slower due to compilation, etc. ... torch.cuda.synchronize()  # Wait for CUDA threads to finish (important!)
for trial in range(num_trials):  # Do it multiple times to capture variance ... Use CUDA events for accurate GPU timing (avoid capturing CPU overhead)
mean_time = mean(times)   # @inspect mean_time @stepover

here's a recipe for success. You benchmark and profile your code. You make changes, and you benchmark your profile, your code again. ... you should always just measure what's going on in your code and figure out what the bottlenecks are before you start writing kernels.
always remember to do your warm-up. ... some things are lazily compiled ... you're going to run it over and over again, so the initial conditions don't really matter.

you often want to time it multiple times because there is some variance. The proper way to time things is to use these CUDA events ... remember to synchronize to wait for the CUDA threads to finish, because everything on the GPU is happening if you have an async.
If you are being very particular, you probably want to maybe look at the whole distribution, the P95 or whatever. But we'll just do the average here.

provenance.filtering_note: torch.utils.benchmark is linked (L164) but not used; the professor rolls his own 'to make benchmarking more transparent' (L165). Defaults are num_warmups=1, num_trials=3 (L179). The CUDA-event versus time.time() distinction is a comment (L190), not demonstrated. The @inspect result at L169 is a GPU measurement and is not reproduced in this thread. Spoken evidence (22:19-22:36): why benchmarking is taught before Triton: 'you should always just measure ... and figure out what the bottlenecks are before you start writing kernels'. Spoken evidence (25:24-25:32): the mean over trials is a simplification; a careful benchmark looks at 'the whole distribution, the P95 or whatever'. The code only says 'Do it multiple times to capture variance' (L189).

external_prerequisites.note: 'Wait for CUDA threads to finish' assumes the learner knows a kernel runs as many threads on the device, separately from the Python process.

misconceptions.belief: Wrapping run() in time.time() calls measures how long the GPU took.
misconceptions.why_wrong: A kernel launch returns to Python immediately; without torch.cuda.synchronize() the stopwatch stops before the GPU has finished, so the measured time is mostly launch overhead (L185, L198).

misconceptions.belief: The first call is as good a measurement as any other.
misconceptions.why_wrong: First calls can include compilation and cache warmup (L181); the steady state is what matters because the kernel will be run many times (L182).

predict.q: You delete torch.cuda.synchronize() at L198 and replace the CUDA events with time.time() around run(). For a large matmul, which way does the measured time move relative to the true GPU time (up or down)?
predict.answer: down, far below the true time
predict.why: The launch is asynchronous: Python returns from run() before the kernel finishes, so the stopwatch captures launch overhead, not execution (L185, L190, L198).
predict.targets_misconception: Wrapping run() in time.time() calls measures how long the GPU took.

transfer.q: A colleague benchmarks naive_gelu, builtin_gelu and torch.compile(naive_gelu) with num_warmups=0 and num_trials=1. Which of the three measurements is most distorted, and in which direction?
transfer.why: With no warmup the single trial includes torch.compile's compilation (L181, L275). The other two have no compile step, so the distortion is concentrated on the compiled version, making it look slower than the naive one.

check.q: You benchmark torch.compile(naive_gelu) with num_trials = 1, then change num_warmups from 0 to 3. What happens to the measured time? Answer up, down or same.
check.answer: down: with no warmup the single trial includes compilation; after warmup it measures only the compiled kernel.
check.why: Warmup absorbs one-off costs such as torch.compile's compilation and cache effects before timing starts (L181-L185, L275).
check.targets_misconception: The first call is as good a measurement as any other.
check.varies: the fix is applied and the learner predicts its effect, instead of spotting the distorted measurement
check.invariant: the first call of a compiled function includes compilation, which warmup removes from the measurement

knowledge_points.label: Matmul time: flat at small dims, then cubic
knowledge_points.statement: Benchmarking a square matmul over dim = 256 ... 8192 shows time roughly constant at small dims, where a fixed per-launch cost dominates and the GPU is mostly idle (the professor: GPUs 'are built for fairly large matrix multiplications'), and then growing like dim³, where the 2·dim³ FLOPs dominate.

anchors.quote: for dim in [256, 512, 1024, 2048, 4096, 8192]: results[dim] = benchmark(run_operation2(dim=dim, operation=lambda a, b: a @ b))  # @inspect results
Note: time is roughly constant when dimension is small, then cubic scaling.

scale up your matrices and see how the time changes. ... it should grow cubically. But notice that there is this flaw where up until you get up to almost 2,000 dimensional matrices, things are basically a constant. ... the shapes of these GPUs are built for fairly large matrix multiplications. And if you have a 2 by 2 matrix, it's going to be very inefficient.

provenance.filtering_note: The professor states the shape of the curve but not where the crossover is; the results dict holds GPU timings from his machine and is not reproduced here. He does not say why the small-dim regime is flat; this thread attributes it to launch overhead in supp-kernel-launch (author inference). Spoken evidence (25:55-26:23), correcting two claims in this note: the crossover is said aloud, flat 'up until you get up to almost 2,000 dimensional matrices' on his B200 (a reading of his own GPU plot, not a portable number); and he does give a reason for the flat regime, 'the shapes of these GPUs are built for fairly large matrix multiplications', i.e. a small matmul cannot fill the hardware. That reason is not launch overhead, which remains this thread's inference (supp-kernel-launch). The two are compatible (an under-filled GPU finishes in roughly fixed time), and the statement was not changed.

external_prerequisites.note: 'Cubic' is 2·dim³ FLOPs; the learner must know the matmul FLOP count to see why.

misconceptions.belief: Matmul time scales with the number of output elements, dim².
misconceptions.why_wrong: Each of the dim² outputs is a length-dim dot product, so FLOPs are 2·dim³ and time follows them once the kernel is compute-bound (L176).

misconceptions.belief: Halving dim always cuts the time by a large factor.
misconceptions.why_wrong: Below the crossover the time is set by a fixed per-launch cost, so dim changes barely move it (L176 'roughly constant').

predict.q: In the cubic regime, you go from dim = 4096 to dim = 8192. The benchmark time multiplies by roughly what factor?
predict.why: FLOPs are 2·dim³; doubling dim multiplies them by 8, and in the compute-bound regime time follows FLOPs (L176).
predict.targets_misconception: Matmul time scales with the number of output elements, dim².

transfer.q: Going from dim = 256 to dim = 512, the measured time barely changes even though FLOPs went up 8x. What is dominating the measurement there, and what does the professor's recipe step before timing (L181-L185) have in common with it?
transfer.answer: A fixed per-call cost (launching the kernel and waiting for it) rather than the arithmetic; the warmup/synchronize step exists because launches are asynchronous and have overhead, the same overhead that floors the small-dim timings.
transfer.why: When the kernel's work is tiny, the time is the launch and completion latency, which does not depend on dim (L176, supp-kernel-launch).

check.q: In the lecture's matmul benchmark, you go from dim = 128 to dim = 256, where the time is dominated by a fixed per-launch cost. What happens to the measured time? Answer up, down or same.
check.answer: same (roughly): at these sizes the fixed launch-and-sync cost dominates, so 8x the FLOPs barely changes the time.
check.why: Small matmuls are overhead-bound: the time is the kernel launch and completion latency, which does not depend on dim. Only at large dims does time grow like dim³ (L172-L176).
check.targets_misconception: Halving dim always cuts the time by a large factor.
check.varies: a pair of small dims, asked as a direction
check.invariant: below the crossover, matmul time is a fixed overhead independent of dim

retrieval.q: Describe the two regimes the professor notes for matmul time versus dimension.
retrieval.answer: Roughly constant at small dimension, then cubic scaling.

retrieval.q: In the cubic regime, which quantity grows as dim³ and sets the time?
retrieval.answer: The FLOP count, 2·dim³ (one multiply-add per (i, j, k) triple).

prompts.self_explain: Why can an 8x increase in FLOPs produce almost no change in measured time at small dims?

presentations.notice: Below about dim 2048 the curve lies on the fixed-cost floor and doubling dim barely moves it; above, each doubling multiplies the time by close to 8 as the 2·dim³ term takes over.

knowledge_points.label: Profiling shows the CUDA kernels behind a PyTorch op
knowledge_points.statement: The PyTorch profiler (ProfilerActivity.CUDA, rows sorted by cuda_time_total) lists which CUDA kernels an op actually launched and how long each ran; the kernel chosen depends on tensor shape, and its name encodes the implementation (cutlass = NVIDIA linear-algebra library, sm100 = Blackwell, f32 = float32, 64x64x16 = tile shape).

anchors.quote: While benchmarking looks at end-to-end time, profiling looks at where time is spent. Independent of time, profiling also helps you understand what's going under the hood.
You can see which CUDA kernels are actually being called (the long names). Different CUDA kernels are invoked depending on the tensor dimensions.

cutlass3x_sm100_simt_sgemm_f32_f32_f32_f32_f32_64x64x16_1x1x1_3_nnn_align1_bi... cutlass: NVIDIA's CUDA library for linear algebra; sm100: corresponds to the NVIDIA Blackwell architecture (B200); f32: float32; 64x64x16: tile shape
torch.profiler.profile(activities=[ProfilerActivity.CUDA], ...) ... prof.key_averages().table(sort_by="cuda_time_total", ...)
Profiling tells you where time is actually spent. ... profiling, even if you don't care about the time, helps you figure out what's actually happening under the hood.
if you change the dimensions-- so now I'm doing a 128 by 128 matmul-- you get actually a different one. If you look closely, that this is 64x64x16, this is 32x32x16.
cutlass is the NVIDIA CUDA library for linear algebra. SM100 corresponds to the Blackwell architecture. ... 64x64x16 is the shape of the tile

provenance.filtering_note: The three tables (add at 2048, matmul at 2048, matmul at 128; L214-L223) are verbatim GPU output appended to var/profiles.txt and exist only in the professor's trace; no kernel durations are quoted here. nsight is deferred to the assignment (L211). 'simt' (no tensor cores) and 'nnn_align1' in the example name are not decoded by the professor. Spoken evidence (28:46-29:02): what 'a different kernel' means concretely: at dim 2048 the matmul kernel's tile is 64x64x16, at dim 128 it is 32x32x16 (read off his profiler tables; a kernel name, not a duration). nsight is deferred to the assignment and skipped (26:55-27:01).

external_prerequisites.note: '64x64x16: tile shape' only means something if the learner knows matmul kernels work on output tiles.

misconceptions.belief: One PyTorch op always maps to one fixed CUDA kernel.
misconceptions.why_wrong: The dispatcher picks a kernel per shape and dtype (L227: different kernels for dim 2048 and dim 128), and a composite op like naive_gelu launches several (L300).

distractor_from: 'the matrix shape' <- misconception: 'One PyTorch op always maps to one fixed CUDA kernel.' (reads the name as describing the problem rather than the chosen implementation)
'the grid size' <- plausible: three numbers look like launch dimensions

knowledge_points.label: GeLU: naive chain of ops vs builtin vs torch.compile
knowledge_points.statement: naive_gelu written as a chain of PyTorch ops launches one kernel per op, each reading and writing HBM; builtin gelu and torch.compile(naive_gelu) run one fused kernel with one HBM read and one write, which is why both are much faster, and the compiled kernel is a Triton kernel.

anchors.quote: 1. Implementation naively from scratch in PyTorch (non-fused) ... 2. Built-in PyTorch implementation (fused) ... 3. Use PyTorch compiler on the naive implementation ... check_equal_1d(naive_gelu, compiled_gelu)
naive_time = benchmark(...) ... builtin_time ... compiled_time ... The builtin and compiled versions are significantly faster!

Naive implementation: multiple kernels, requires many reads/writes from/to HBM (no fusion). Builtin and compiled versions: one kernel (kernel fusion), one read from HBM, one write to HBM. The compiled kernel is a Triton kernel.
you can take any PyTorch function, you call torch.compile on it, and it generates another function. And it does the same thing.

Built-in is much faster and compiled is much faster as well, but not maybe as quite as fast as built-in. ... They all compute the same answer, but they have wildly different performance characteristics.
the reason this is slow is that when you launch a kernel, the kernel has to read from HBM. ... between kernel invocations, things have to go back to HBM.
why does this exist? Well, because people use GeLU. So someone wrote a kernel for it and put it in the standard library.
The compiled kernel is one Triton kernel, and this is slower than the built-in. ... it's very hardware dependent. And I think none of this is terribly optimized.

provenance.filtering_note: naive_time, builtin_time and compiled_time are GPU measurements; only the direction is recorded: naive slowest, builtin and compiled 'significantly faster' (L283). The three profiler tables (L288-L297) that show the kernel counts are verbatim GPU output. The professor never counts naive_gelu's kernels; from L697 the expression has on the order of eight elementwise ops, so 'multiple' is left as stated. check_equal_1d uses atol=1e-6 (L713). Spoken evidence (32:09, 36:18-36:48): the order is builtin fastest, compiled close behind, naive slowest; asked why, he says the compiled Triton kernel 'is slower than the built-in', that last year it 'was actually closer', and that it is 'very hardware dependent'. The naive time is read aloud (32:00-32:05) and, by this thread's rule, not quoted. Spoken evidence (33:23-33:54): the reason given for naive's slowness is the round trip, 'between kernel invocations, things have to go back to HBM'; the built-in exists simply 'because people use GeLU' (34:08). How torch.compile works is skipped (34:24).

prerequisites.note: The explanation is read off the profiler: many rows versus one row.

external_prerequisites.note: Lecture 5 introduced fusion on slides; here it is observed in a profile.
Why fewer HBM round trips mean less time: GeLU is memory-bound.

misconceptions.belief: builtin_gelu is faster because it uses a cheaper formula with fewer FLOPs.
misconceptions.why_wrong: It uses the same tanh approximation (L702) and is checked equal to naive_gelu (L272). The saving is one kernel instead of many, i.e. one HBM read and write instead of one per op (L300-L301).

misconceptions.belief: torch.compile speeds things up by changing the arithmetic.
misconceptions.why_wrong: The professor checks compiled_gelu against naive_gelu precisely because 'compilation shouldn't change semantics' (L277); it changes the kernel count, not the math.

predict.q: naive_gelu launches about k elementwise kernels on a 16384x16384 tensor; builtin_gelu launches one. The op is memory-bound. The ratio naive_time / builtin_time is closest to which?
predict.why: Each unfused kernel moves the whole tensor through HBM at least once, so bytes moved, and hence time, scale with the kernel count; the FLOPs are the same either way (L300-L301).
predict.targets_misconception: builtin_gelu is faster because it uses a cheaper formula with fewer FLOPs.

transfer.q: You write a sigmoid-based GeLU as a chain of four PyTorch ops in the same style as naive_gelu. Without compiling, how does its kernel count and HBM traffic compare with naive_gelu's, and what single change brings it to builtin-level speed?
transfer.answer: Fewer kernels (about four instead of about eight) and proportionally fewer HBM round trips, so faster but still unfused; torch.compile fuses the chain into one Triton kernel with one read and one write.
transfer.why: The cost is per launched kernel, each with its own HBM read and write; fusion removes all but one (L300-L302).

check.q: A memory-bound chain of 6 elementwise PyTorch ops runs on a 8192 × 8192 fp32 tensor, each op reading one tensor and writing one. torch.compile fuses the chain into one kernel with one read and one write. By what factor does HBM traffic fall? Type only the number.
check.why: Unfused: 6 kernels × (one read + one write) = 12 tensor transfers. Fused: 2. 12 / 2 = 6. The arithmetic is unchanged; the saving is the round trips to HBM (L300-L302).
check.targets_misconception: torch.compile speeds things up by changing the arithmetic.
check.varies: the number of ops in the chain and an explicit traffic ratio
check.invariant: each unfused elementwise op costs one HBM read and write; fusion leaves one of each

retrieval.q: How many HBM reads and writes does the fused GeLU do, versus the naive chain?
retrieval.answer: Fused: one read and one write. Naive: one read and write per kernel, many kernels.

retrieval.q: Which compiler produces the kernel behind torch.compile(naive_gelu)?
retrieval.answer: Triton (the compiled kernel is a Triton kernel).

retrieval.q: Which check does the professor run before benchmarking the compiled version, and what is the stated reason?
retrieval.answer: check_equal_1d(naive_gelu, compiled_gelu); compilation should not change semantics.

prompts.self_explain: Why does fusing leave the FLOP count unchanged yet cut the time by a large factor?

presentations.notice: Five kernel launches, each with its own HBM read and write, collapse into one launch with a single read and a single write; the arithmetic between them is unchanged.
listen for: why each kernel boundary sends the tensor back to HBM
listen for: compiled Triton is slower than the built-in here, and the gap is hardware dependent

knowledge_points.label: CUDA programs threads; Triton programs thread blocks
knowledge_points.statement: In CUDA you specify what each thread does (fine-grained control, but you manage shared memory and more yourself); in Triton you specify what each thread block does, following the frame: load data into shared memory, operate on it, write back to global memory.

anchors.quote: In CUDA (developed by NVIDIA), specify what each thread does. Pros: fine-grained control. Cons: need to manage more things (e.g., shared memory)
In Triton (developed by OpenAI), specify what each thread block does. ... Conceptual framework: load data into shared memory, operate on it, write back to global memory

for non-elementwise operations like softmax or matrix multiplication, threads need to communicate. Reading/writing from HBM is slow, so use shared memory (local to SM). ... In Triton, think natively in terms of thread blocks (later).
Programming model: grid (HBM) -> thread block (shared memory) -> thread (registers)
why do we have thread blocks? ... for operations that involve communicating with threads, such as softmax or matrix multiplication, this view isn't really enough.

it could be enough if you were willing to pay the cost of writing and reading HBM. ... use shared memory, which is local to SM. ... a collection of threads that are all going to access this shared memory.

if you were to write in CUDA ... the mental model is, what does each thread do? ... it's very closely related to what is actually happening underneath the hood. And it's fine-grained, gives you fine-grained control.

some operations require them to communicate. So what has to happen is that they have to synchronize. ... you have to basically do that bookkeeping. So if you were doing all element-wise operations, this CUDA is just fine.

Triton was developed by OpenAI. ... You basically specify what each thread block does. ... If you really go and want to exploit every single new feature of the latest hardware, it might not give you the full flexibility.
for this element wise, it looks pretty much the same, right. And in fact, CUDA is even, I think, simpler, because it really is element wise.
things are easier to think about thread blocks than individual threads, because you don't have to think about explicitly synchronizing threads or doing shared memory.
every language has an inductive bias ... Triton was built by people who train transformers. So anything involving transformers, I think it's going to be relatively easy there.

provenance.filtering_note: No CUDA code is shown; the comparison is two bullet lists. What Triton automates inside a block (thread-to-element mapping, shared-memory allocation, coalescing, warp-level reductions) is left implicit and only surfaces when the PTX is inspected (L334). Triton's own word for a block's instance, 'program', appears only as tl.program_id. Spoken evidence (37:47-38:32, 46:33-47:14): where each language pays: for purely elementwise work 'this CUDA is just fine' and even 'simpler'; CUDA's cost appears when threads must communicate, because then 'they have to synchronize' and 'you have to basically do that bookkeeping', which Triton hides (1:23:16-1:23:38). Its limit is also said: for 'every single new feature of the latest hardware, it might not give you the full flexibility' (38:46). Spoken evidence (5:19-5:48): thread blocks are not logically required for communication, only for speed: threads 'could' communicate through HBM 'if you were willing to pay the cost', which is too slow.

prerequisites.note: Motivation: the compiled kernel the profiler showed is a Triton kernel; now write one by hand.

external_prerequisites.note: Thread, block, grid and the fact that a block shares one SM's shared memory.

misconceptions.belief: Each line of a Triton kernel is executed by a single thread on a single element.
misconceptions.why_wrong: A Triton program is one whole thread block: tl.arange produces a BLOCK_SIZE-wide vector that the compiler spreads across the block's threads (eight elements per thread in the GeLU PTX, L334).

predict.q: In triton_gelu_kernel, the line x = tl.load(x_ptr + offsets, mask=mask) (L379) is executed on behalf of how much of the hardware: one thread, one warp, or the whole thread block?
choices: one thread, loading the single element at its offset
one warp, the 32 threads that issue the load together
the whole thread block, loading BLOCK_SIZE elements at once
predict.answer: the whole thread block, loading BLOCK_SIZE elements at once
distractor_from: 'one thread' <- misconception: 'Each line of a Triton kernel is executed by a single thread on a single element.'
'one warp' <- plausible: carries CUDA's warp-level SIMT picture over to Triton's block-level programs
predict.why: Triton code describes what a block does (L312); offsets is a BLOCK_SIZE-element vector and the load is the block's collective read.
predict.targets_misconception: Each line of a Triton kernel is executed by a single thread on a single element.

transfer.q: You port the softmax kernel to a model where you must decide which thread holds which column and insert a barrier before computing the row maximum. Which of the two programming models is that, and which single Triton line hides that work in the lecture's kernel?
transfer.answer: CUDA; tl.max(x_row, axis=0) at L476 performs the cross-thread reduction with no explicit thread mapping or barrier.
transfer.why: Per-thread programming exposes communication inside the block; per-block programming lets the compiler handle it (L309-L310 versus L312-L314).

check.q: Writing the lecture's softmax in CUDA instead of Triton, which of these must you write yourself that Triton's tl.max(x_row, axis=0) handles for you?
choices: the cross-thread reduction and its sync
the pointer arithmetic for the row
the launch grid of one program per row
check.answer: the cross-thread reduction and its sync
distractor_from: 'pointer arithmetic for the row' <- misconception: 'Each line of a Triton kernel is executed by a single thread on a single element.' (Triton code still does its own pointer arithmetic per block)
'the mask for out-of-range columns' <- plausible: Triton kernels write masks explicitly too

knowledge_points.label: The Triton GeLU kernel line by line
knowledge_points.statement: The GeLU kernel loads one block of x with a mask, computes 0.5·x·(1 + tanh(0.79788456·(x + 0.044715·x³))) on that block with tanh built from exp (tanh a = (e^{2a} − 1)/(e^{2a} + 1), because tl.tanh does not exist), and stores with the same mask: one HBM read and one write per element, every intermediate stays on-chip.

tl.store(y_ptr + offsets, y, mask=mask)

knowledge_points.statement: The Triton softmax launches one program per row (grid (M,)), sets BLOCK_SIZE = next_power_of_2(N) so a whole row fits in one block, reaches the row through x_ptr + row_idx * x_row_stride, loads with mask col < num_cols and other=-inf so padding contributes exp(-inf) = 0, reduces with tl.max and tl.sum over axis 0, and stores the row with the same mask.

x_row = x_row - tl.max(x_row, axis=0); numerator = tl.exp(x_row); denominator = tl.sum(numerator, axis=0); y_row = numerator / denominator
y_start_ptr = y_ptr + row_idx * y_row_stride; ... tl.store(y_ptrs, y_row, mask=col_offsets < num_cols)

knowledge_points.label: Matmul: naive O(1) intensity, tiling gives O(tile_size)
knowledge_points.statement: A naive matmul reads A[m, k] and B[k, n] from HBM for every (m, n, k): MKN reads and O(1) arithmetic intensity; loading all of A and B into shared memory would give MK + KN reads but does not fit; tiling loads one A tile and one B tile per step into shared memory and reuses each across a whole output tile, for O(tile_size) intensity.

Key idea: divide the matrix C into output tiles (thread blocks). Fix an output tile in C. For each pair of (row tile of A, column tile of B): Load the corresponding A tile and B tile from HBM into shared memory. Perform matrix multiplication on the tiles. Accumulate ... Arithmetic intensity: O(tile_size).

knowledge_points.label: Supplement: memory-bound elementwise ops and what fusion buys
knowledge_points.statement: An elementwise op on a large tensor is memory-bound (a few FLOPs per element against bytes moved), so its time is set by bytes through HBM, not FLOPs; a chain of k unfused elementwise ops moves the tensor through HBM about k times while a fused kernel moves it once, so fusion's speedup is on the order of the eliminated round trips, and extra arithmetic inside the fused kernel is nearly free.

Naive implementation: multiple kernels, requires many reads/writes from/to HBM (no fusion). Builtin and compiled versions: one kernel (kernel fusion), one read from HBM, one write to HBM.
Triton: think in terms of thread blocks (read to shared memory, do stuff (fusion), write back HBM)
naive implementation. Multiple kernels requires multiple reads and writes to and from HBM. There's no kernel fusion here. This is slow. ... you read from HBM once, you write to HBM once per element.
